title: HCI Interaction Design Models — MHP, KLM, GOMS, Fitts, Hick, STN, Three-State Model
description: Exam revision: every concept from the Interaction Design Models deck, visualised.
endCard: 📘 Interaction Design Models — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: Predict user behaviour before a single real user arrives

lines: Can we predict how long a user will take, before a single real user ever touches the design?
That is the promise of interaction design models.
We'll cover the Model Human Processor, the Keystroke Level Model, GOMS, Fitts' law, Hick's law, state transition networks, and the three state model.

scenes.title: 1. Predictive vs descriptive models

items.b:
e.g. Model Human Processor (MHP), Keyboard Level Model (KLM)

Approximate user actions before real users are brought into testing

e.g. State Transition Networks, Three-State Model

A framework for thinking about interaction — how people interact with dynamic systems

lines: Models come in two families.
Predictive models, like the Model Human Processor and the Keyboard Level Model, are a priori, meaning pre-experience.
They give approximations of user actions before real users are brought into the testing environment.
Descriptive models, like state networks and the Three State Model, give a framework for thinking about interaction.
They help us understand how people interact with dynamic systems.

scenes.title: 2. MHP — memories and processors

items.b:
Sensors: eyes, ears, touch, taste
Buffers (sensory image stores):
VIS visual · AIS auditory
HIS haptic · TIS taste

Working memory (WM)
Short-term memory
Long-term memory (LTM)

arm–hand–finger system
head–eye system
leg–foot–toe system

lines: The Model Human Processor makes general predictions about human performance.
It is a predictive model, described by a set of memories and processors that work according to principles of operation.
The perceptual system has sensors, eyes, ears, touch and taste,
and buffers called sensory image stores: the visual, auditory, haptic and taste memory stores.
The cognitive system holds working memory, short term memory and long term memory.
The motor system acts through the arm hand finger system, the head eye system, and the leg foot toe system.

scenes.title: 3. MHP — follow one signal
lines: Follow one signal. Your eyes and ears feed the perceptual processor.
It drops the stimulus into the visual and auditory image stores, then into working memory.
The cognitive processor works between working memory and long term memory,
and the motor processor turns the decision into movement of arms, wrists and fingers.
Sense, perceive, store, think, recall, act.

scenes.title: 4. Working memory and chunks

items.b: Working memory is a subset of “activated” elements from long-term memory
Sensory image stores (VIS, AIS…) encode only physical parameters of the stimulus
Shortly after stimulus onset, a symbolic representation is registered in WM
The activated elements from LTM are called chunks

letters in a word → one chunk
several words of a well-known phrase → one chunk
Chunks in WM can interfere with each other due to LTM associations

lines: Working memory consists of a subset of activated elements from long term memory.
The sensory image stores encode only non-symbolic, physical parameters of the stimulus.
Shortly after the stimulus begins, a symbolic representation is registered in working memory.
The activated elements from long term memory are called chunks.
A chunk can be made of smaller units, like the letters of a word, or of several words, as in a well known phrase.
Chunks in working memory can interfere with each other, because of long term memory associations.

scenes.title: 5. Long-term memory

nodes.b: can add items to WM — but NOT directly to LTM
WM must interact with LTM for a significant time before storage
this increases the number of retrieval cues
items with numerous associations are more likely to be retrieved

lines: The cognitive processor can add items to working memory, but not to long term memory.
Working memory must interact with long term memory over a significant length of time before an item can be stored there.
This increases the number of cues that can be used to retrieve the item later.
So items with numerous associations have a greater probability of being retrieved.

scenes.title: 6. The three processors

items.b:
captures sensations via visual + auditory channels
• visual decay shorter than auditory
• cycle time varies with stimulus
• τp = 50–200 ms

bridges perceptual ↔ motor
• simple conduit OR learning, fact retrieval, problem solving
• WM coding: visual + auditory
• LTM coding: associative, semantic
• WM decay: wide range, sensitive to # chunks
• LTM decay: infinite

converts thought into action
• cycle time counted in discrete micro-movements
• τm = 30–100 ms

lines: Now the three processors.
The perceptual processor captures physical sensations through the visual and auditory receptor channels.
Perceptual decay is shorter for the visual channel than for the auditory channel.
Its cycle time varies with the nature of the stimulus: fifty to two hundred milliseconds.
The cognitive processor bridges the perceptual and motor systems.
It can be a simple conduit, or involve complex processes like learning, fact retrieval and problem solving.
Cognitive coding in working memory is mainly visual and auditory. In long term memory it is associative, mainly semantic.
Working memory decay has a large range and is very sensitive to the number of chunks. Long term memory decay is infinite.
The motor processor converts thought into action. Its cycle time is counted in discrete micro-movements.

scenes.title: 7. Timing values to memorise

cells:
WM 5–226 s (1 chunk 73 s, 3 chunks 7 s)
LTM: lifetime

lines: Here are the timing values to memorise.
Perceptual processor: visual decay ninety to one thousand milliseconds, auditory decay nine hundred to thirty-five hundred.
Sensory store capacity is seven to seventeen letters visual, and five letters auditory. Cycle time, fifty to two hundred milliseconds.
Cognitive processor: working memory decays in five to two hundred twenty-six seconds. One chunk lasts seventy-three seconds, three chunks only seven.
Long term memory decay is a lifetime. Working memory stores two to four chunks, and long term memory is infinite.
Cognitive cycle time is twenty-five to one hundred seventy milliseconds.
Motor processor cycle time, thirty to one hundred milliseconds.
Add all three cycles: response time is one hundred five to four hundred seventy milliseconds.

scenes.title: 8. Cognition example
lines: A cognition example on perception and long term memory interaction.
Read out the ink colours of these words, and time it. Call it T one.
Now read these colour names. Time it, T two. Perception speed: T one is greater than T two.
In the first list, word meaning from long term memory fights the colour you perceive, so you slow down.
Finally, read this. The cat. The two middle letters are the same shape, yet you read H, then A.
Different interpretations, why? Because memory is associative. Context decides.

scenes.title: 9. MHP principles P0–P3

items.b: each cognitive cycle triggers interaction WM → LTM (WM ← LTM chunk)
varies inversely with stimulus intensity — loud noise, electric shock = faster
perceived info (visual, aural, tactile) is encoded before LTM storage; encoding decides its access cues
number of cognitive cycles is context dependent; retrieval difficulty depends on the cues presented

lines: The MHP runs on principles of operation. Principle zero: the cognitive processor's recognize act cycle.
Each cycle triggers interaction from working memory to long term memory, pulling a chunk into working memory.
Principle one: perceptual cycle time varies inversely with stimulus intensity. A loud noise or an electric shock is perceived faster.
Principle two: encoding. Perceived information is encoded before it is stored in long term memory, and the encoding decides how it maps to access cues.
Principle three: discrimination. The number of cycles is context dependent, and retrieval from long term memory depends on the cues presented.

scenes.title: 10. P4 — variable rate & practice

viz.name: practice
viz.left:
P4 · Cognitive Processor Rate
Variable Rate Principle
• cycle time Tc shorter with increased task demand / info load (panic!)
• Tc also diminishes with practice
n = attempts · T1 = initial time · Tn = time at nth repetition

lines: Principle four: the cognitive processor rate, also called the variable rate principle.
Cycle time gets shorter when greater effort is demanded, like in a panic situation, and it also shrinks with practice.
The performance gain from practice follows a power law. T n equals T one times n to the power minus alpha.
Here n is the number of attempts, T one is the initial time, and T n the time at the n-th repetition. Alpha lies between point two and point six.

scenes.title: 11. P7 — uncertainty & Hick's law

rows.t: Decision time ↑ as uncertainty ↑ → more cognitive cycles
H = entropy of the decision · k = constant

lines: Principle seven: the uncertainty principle.
Decision time increases with uncertainty about the judgment to be made, because it needs more cognitive cycles.
This is Hick's law of choice reaction time: T equals k times H, where H is the entropy of the decision and k is a constant.
In general, H is the sum of p i times log base two of one over p i, plus one.
If all n alternatives are equally likely, H is just log base two of n plus one.

scenes.title: 12. Keystroke (Keyboard) Level Model

items.b: practical design tool — captures & calculates the physical actions to complete a task; finds the most efficient method for a context
a task (maybe subtasks) · the system's command language · user's motor skill parameters · response time parameters
time an expert user takes to execute the task — provided they make no errors
Operators · Encoding methods · Heuristics for placing M (mental) operators

lines: Next, the Keyboard Level Model, better known as the Keystroke Level Model.
It is a practical design tool that captures and calculates the physical actions a user must carry out to complete a task.
It helps find the most efficient method, and judge its suitability for specific contexts.
Given a task, the system's command language, the user's motor skill parameters and the response time parameters,
it predicts the time an expert user will take to execute the task, provided they use the method without error.
The KLM is made of operators, encoding methods, and heuristics for placing mental operators.

scenes.title: 13. KLM operators: K P H D M R

letters.d:
press a key or button
0.08 – 1.20 s

hands to keyboard or device
0.4 s

lines: Six operators. K: press a key or button, from point zero eight to one point two seconds.
P: point with the mouse, about one point one seconds, from Fitts' law.
H: home the hands on the keyboard or another device, point four seconds.
D: draw line segments, point nine times the number of segments, plus point one six times their total length.
M: mental preparation, one point three five seconds.
R: system response, which depends on the system and the activity.
Memory hook: Keep Pointing Home, Draw, Mind the Response.

scenes.title: 14. K depends on typing skill
lines: K changes with typing skill. Pressing a modifier key like shift counts as a separate operation.
Best typist, one hundred thirty-five words per minute: point zero eight seconds.
Good typist, ninety words per minute: point one two. Average skilled typist, fifty-five words per minute: point two.
Average non-secretary typist, forty words per minute: point two eight.
Typing random letters: point five. Typing complex codes: point seven five.
Worst typist, unfamiliar with the keyboard: one point two seconds.
P ranges from point eight to one point five seconds and does not include the button click. H is point four, M is one point three five.

scenes.title: 15. Encoding methods

rows.t: long form: MK[i] K[p] K[c] K[o] K[n] K[f] K[i] K[g] K[RETURN]
H[mouse] MP[Network icon] K[Right click] P[Prepare] K[Left click]

lines: Encoding methods define how the operators of a task are written.
Typing ipconfig in a command window is M, then a K for each letter, and K for return.
In short-hand, it's M, eight K, ipconfig return.
That's one point three five plus eight times point two, which is two point nine five seconds for an average skilled typist.
Using Windows Network, then Repair: H mouse, M P network icon, K right click, P prepare, K left click. Four point three five seconds.

scenes.title: 16. KLM example: mirtake → mistake

nodes.b: position after the bad char, click
reposition the insertion point · total ≈ 6.9 s (illustrative, K = 0.2)

lines: Example two. Correct the typo mirtake into mistake.
Move hand to mouse, H. Position the mouse after the bad character and click, P K left.
Return to keyboard, H. Delete the bad character, M K backspace.
Type the new character, K. Then reposition the insertion point, H, M, P, K left.
With K at point two, that totals roughly six point nine seconds. That total is illustrative.

scenes.title: 17. Calculating P with Fitts' law

rows.t: A = distance to target · W = width (cross-section) of target
a, b depend on the input device — found by regression (here a = 0, b = 0.1)
🖱️ middle of 19 cm screen → 2 cm toolbar at top

lines: Where does P come from? Experiments give an average of one point one seconds, based on Fitts' law.
P equals a plus b, times log base two of A over W, plus one.
A is the distance from the target, and W is its width. a and b depend on the input device, and are found by regression.
Example: the mouse is in the middle of a nineteen centimetre screen, and must reach a two centimetre toolbar at the top.
With a zero and b point one, that's point one times log two of ten point five, about point four seconds.

scenes.title: 18. Menus: Mac vs Windows
lines: Fitts' law explains menu placement.
On the Mac, the menu is aligned with the screen edge, with no offset. Users can't overshoot, so they need not be accurate. The target acts about fifty millimetres tall.
On Windows, the pull-down menu is offset by the title bar, so it needs more accuracy. The target is only five millimetres wide.
With distance eighty millimetres, a fifty and b one fifty: the Mac takes about two hundred fifty-six milliseconds, Windows about six hundred sixty-three.
Edge targets are effectively infinite in size, so they are fast.

scenes.title: 19. Rules for placing M

items.b: M before every K that enters new text and every P that selects a command

M fully anticipated by previous operator → delete
PMK → PK
string of M's → delete all but the first
M<cmd>K M<arg>K → M<cmd>K <arg>K

K ends a command → delete M
K ends an argument → keep M

lines: KLM operators are physical or cognitive. Physical ones come from the method, like clicking an icon. The mental M follows heuristics.
Rule zero: place M in front of every K that enters new text, and every P that selects a command.
Rule one: if M is anticipated by the previous operator, delete it. P M K becomes P K.
Rule two: in a string of M's, delete all except the first.
Rule three: if K is a redundant terminator, delete the M in front of it.
Rule four: delete M if K terminates a command string, but keep M if K terminates an argument string.

scenes.title: 20. KLM limits & applications

items.b: Errors · Learning · Functionality · Recall · Concentration · Fatigue · Acceptability
“Every Lazy Fox Really Can't Feel Anything”
mouse-driven text editor — KLMs served as expert proxies during development
showed the trade-off between keystrokes in the query and number of returned fields

lines: The KLM was not designed to consider errors, learning, functionality, recall, concentration, fatigue, or acceptability.
Memory hook: Every Lazy Fox Really Can't Feel Anything.
Applications. Case one: in developing the Xerox Star, a mouse driven text editor, KLMs served as expert proxies.
Case two: for a directory assistance workstation, the KLM clarified the trade-off between keystrokes in the query and the number of returned fields.

scenes.title: 21. GOMS

letters.d: tasks broken into goals and sub-goals
the specific actions needed to carry out the task
ways of achieving a goal, made of operators
decide which method the user chooses

lines: GOMS: goals, operators, methods and selection rules. Goal and task models explore the methods people use.
Card and colleagues suggested describing interaction as the sequential actions a person takes to accomplish a task.
Goals: tasks are deconstructed into a set of goals and sub-goals.
Operators: tasks can only be done by undertaking specific actions.
Methods represent ways of achieving a goal, made of operators.
Selection rules determine which method the user chooses.

scenes.title: 22. GOMS family

items.b:
Card, Moran & Newell — detailed expansion of GOMS with analysis procedures & notation
• predicts behaviour
• judges memory needs (depth of nested goals)
• insight into performance

Natural GOMS Language (Kieras, 1997) — structured natural-language notation
• measures time to learn a method
• checks consistency of methods

Cognitive, Perceptual, Motor operators
• PERT charts + critical path method
• based directly on MHP
• processors work in parallel

lines: There's a whole family of GOMS models.
CMN GOMS, named after Card, Moran and Newell, is a detailed expansion of GOMS, with specific analysis procedures and notation.
It can predict behaviour, judge memory requirements from the depth of nested goal structures, and give insight into performance.
NGOMSL, the Natural GOMS Language by Kieras, gives a structured natural language notation and analysis procedure.
It measures the time to learn a specific method of operation, and checks the consistency of a design's methods.
CPM GOMS represents cognitive, perceptual and motor operators.

scenes.title: 23. CPM-GOMS & PERT charts
lines: CPM GOMS uses PERT charts, the Program Evaluation Review Technique, and maps task durations with the critical path method.
It is based directly on the Model Human Processor, and assumes perceptual, cognitive and motor processors work in parallel. Start eye move, move eyes to target, perceive target, verify paragraph.
The longest chain of dependent operators is the critical path, and it sets the total time.

scenes.title: 24. Modeling structure — Hick's law
lines: Structural models show the relationship between conceptual and physical components, so we can judge a design's effectiveness.
Hick's law can be used to create menu structures.
The time to choose one item from n alternatives is proportional to log base two of the number of choices, plus one.
The coefficients come from experiments. Raskin suggests a equals fifty and b equals one fifty, for back of the envelope estimates.
So a menu of seven equally likely items takes about five hundred milliseconds.
The equation assumes every item has an equal probability of being chosen.

scenes.title: 25. Other forms of Hick's law

viz.f: H = log<sub>2</sub>(n + 1) → T = a + b log<sub>2</sub>(n + 1)

rows.t: different probabilities p<sub>j</sub>: H = Σ p<sub>j</sub> log<sub>2</sub>(1/p<sub>j</sub> + 1)
generalises to: T = c + d · Σ p<sub>j</sub> log<sub>2</sub>(1/p<sub>j</sub> + 1)
📋 Menu order must be logical & relevant
rules not understood → arrangement looks random → slow linear, sequential search

lines: For n equally probable alternatives, H equals log two of n plus one, so T equals a plus b log two of n plus one.
For n alternatives, each with a different probability p j, H is the sum of p j log two of one over p j, plus one.
This generalises to c plus d times that sum.
Menus are lists grouped by some system, so the listing order must be logical and relevant. If users don't understand the rules, they search in a slow, linear, sequential way.

scenes.title: 26. Modeling dynamics — STNs
lines: Modeling dynamics. Interaction is a feedback loop: user actions alter the system's state, which influences the user's next action.
State transition networks explore how a system moves between states. Use them for menus, icons, tools, and to show how peripheral devices operate.
They are appropriate for sequential operations that involve choice by the user,
and for expressing iteration, looping back to repeat a step.

scenes.title: 27. Three-State Model
lines: The three state model helps designers choose appropriate input devices for an interaction design.
It reveals a device's intrinsic states and transitions, so devices without the right states can be ruled out early.
Tracked: the mouse is tracked and shown as the cursor. Dragged: the mouse manipulates elements with drag and drop.
Disengaged: a light pen or a finger on a touch screen moves without being tracked, then re-engages anywhere. Lifting a mouse does the same.
Tracked, dragged, and disengaged: three kinds of pointer movement.

scenes.title: Recap

viz.s: MHP · K P H D M R · GOMS · Fitts · Hick · STN · TSM

lines: Quick recap.
MHP: perceptual, cognitive and motor processors. KLM operators: K, P, H, D, M, R. GOMS: goals, operators, methods, selection rules.
Fitts for pointing, Hick for choosing, state networks and the three state model for dynamics. You've got this.
